analysis.one_liner: Bars EPA from issuing health rules unless all underlying science data is made publicly available.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 228-194 on March 29, 2017, with 225 of 236 Republicans in favor; the Senate never voted, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the EPA from proposing or finalizing any regulation, standard, or assessment unless every piece of scientific data behind it is posted online in enough detail for outsiders to reproduce the research. Health records and other confidential data could be released to anyone who signs a confidentiality agreement. The EPA would have only $1 million a year to comply. Supporters called this transparency; the practical effect is that landmark studies relying on confidential patient data could no longer be used to set pollution limits.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries regulated by the EPA, especially chemical, coal, and oil and gas companies, gain the most: rules they oppose would become far harder to write, because the studies linking pollution to disease often cannot be made public without breaking promises to patients. Companies could also obtain raw patient health records by signing a confidentiality agreement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated chemical, coal, and oil companies

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the EPA from proposing, finalizing, or issuing any regulation, standard, or assessment unless all scientific and technical information behind it is publicly available online in a way that allows 'substantial reproduction' of the research.

Allows personally identifiable health information, trade secrets, and confidential commercial data to be disclosed to any person who signs a written confidentiality agreement with the EPA Administrator.
Caps what the EPA can spend carrying out the requirement at $1 million per fiscal year, drawn from otherwise authorized appropriations.
Supporters' stated goal was transparency: research funded by taxpayers would be open to independent analysis and replication.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who breathe polluted air or drink contaminated water: EPA health standards rest on epidemiological studies whose raw data is confidential patient information, so those studies could be excluded from rulemaking, weakening protections. Patients would also face having their private medical records handed to industry representatives who sign an agreement.
analysis.who_pays_short: People exposed to pollution; patients in health studies

drawbacks.text: Major studies that established links between air pollution and premature death rely on confidential patient records that cannot be published without breaking privacy commitments to participants; the bill would prohibit the EPA from relying on such studies, undercutting the scientific basis for clean air rules.
The $1 million annual cap is far too small to digitize, redact, and publish decades of research data, so the EPA could not realistically comply and would simply have to stop issuing rules.
The confidentiality-agreement provision would let outside parties, including company lawyers, view raw personal health data that study participants were promised would stay private.

The good-faith case for the bill: when government restricts private conduct based on science the public cannot see, independent replication builds trust, and some data can be shared with privacy safeguards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency goal sounds reasonable, but the bill was designed so that the studies EPA rules actually depend on — confidential patient records — could not be used, and the $1 million budget made compliance impossible in practice. The cost would fall on public health protections, while regulated industries gained a procedural veto over new rules.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote, but the Senate referred it to its Environment and Public Works Committee and never brought it up before that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced March 8, 2017 and reported by the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee 17-12 within three weeks.
The House passed it 228-194 on March 29, 2017, with 225 of 236 Republicans voting yes and only 3 of 193 Democrats.

A Democratic motion to recommit — instructing that the EPA must use the best available science when responding to threats to public health — failed 189-232, with 188 of 193 Democrats in favor and 1 of 236 Republicans.
The Senate received the bill March 30, 2017 and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where no vote ever occurred.
The bill never became law; it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: EPA's ability to rely on confidential-data health studies in rulemaking was left intact, so the public's existing air and water protections stood. The industries that would have gained a new tool to block pollution rules did not get it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public health protections; EPA rulemaking authority

for.name: Rep. Lamar Smith
for.role: Chair, House Science, Space, and Technology Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, brought it through his committee, and reported it to the House three weeks after introduction.

for.name: House Science, Space, and Technology Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a markup one day after introduction and ordered the bill reported 17-12.

against.name: Rep. Donald McEachin
against.what_they_did: Offered a motion to recommit instructing the committee to add a requirement that the EPA use the best available science when responding to public health threats; it failed 189-232.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a vote on it before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost entirely by party: 225 of 236 Republicans yes, 3 of 193 Democrats yes on passage; the failed motion to recommit was the mirror image, 188 of 193 Democrats yes and 1 of 236 Republicans.

industries.industry: Chemical, coal, and oil and gas companies
industries.note: The bill would have made it nearly impossible for the EPA to rely on epidemiological studies with confidential patient data — the foundation of major air and water pollution rules — giving regulated industries a way to stall or defeat new standards. The confidentiality-agreement provision would also have opened participants' raw health records to company representatives.

industries.industry: Academic health researchers and study participants
industries.note: Researchers' long-term cohort studies depend on promises that patient data stays private; the bill would disqualify that data from EPA use and allow it to be released under confidentiality agreements, threatening both the research and the participants' privacy.
